title: Network Flow Foundations, Residual Graphs & Reductions

questions.prompt: Which condition defines a valid $s$-$t$ flow in a network?
options: Capacity: $0 \le f(e) \le c(e)$ for every edge, plus flow conservation at every vertex except $s$ and $t$.
Every edge must be saturated.
Flow must be integral.
At each vertex, the total flow in must equal zero.
questions.explanation: A flow respects edge capacities and conserves flow at internal vertices (inflow = outflow). Edges need not be saturated, and integrality is a consequence (integrality theorem), not a definition.

questions.prompt: Network: $s\to a$ (3), $s\to b$ (2), $a\to t$ (2), $b\to t$ (2), $a\to b$ (1). What is the maximum flow value from $s$ to $t$? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: The cut $\{s,a,b\}$ vs $\{t\}$ has capacity $c(a,t)+c(b,t)=2+2=4$, so max flow $\le 4$. It is achievable: send $s\to a\to t$ 2 units and $s\to b\to t$ 2 units. Hence max flow $= 4$.

questions.prompt: Why must the residual graph contain a **reverse edge** for each original edge?
options: To double the network size for no reason.
To allow the algorithm to cancel flow along an edge: pushing flow on the reverse residual edge reduces the flow on the original edge.
Because capacities can be negative.
To store the original capacity.
questions.explanation: Reverse edges with residual capacity equal to the current flow let augmenting paths re-route earlier (possibly suboptimal) flow, enabling the algorithm to recover from bad choices and reach the true maximum.

questions.prompt: Left side $\{1,2,3\}$, right side $\{a,b,c\}$, edges $1{-}a, 1{-}b, 2{-}a, 3{-}b, 3{-}c$. What is the size of a maximum bipartite matching? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: A perfect matching exists: $1{-}b$, $2{-}a$, $3{-}c$, matching all three left vertices. So the maximum matching size is $3$.

questions.prompt: Which statements about network flow are TRUE?
options: If all capacities are integers, there is a maximum flow in which every edge carries an integer amount (integrality theorem).
The value of a maximum flow equals the capacity of a minimum cut (Max-Flow Min-Cut theorem).
Ford-Fulkerson with arbitrary augmenting paths may fail to terminate if capacities are irrational.
Every maximum flow saturates every edge of the network.
questions.explanation: Integrality, Max-Flow Min-Cut, and the non-termination issue with irrational capacities on bad augmenting-path choices are all true. Not every edge is saturated in a max flow (D false) — only the forward edges of a specific min cut need be saturated.

questions.prompt: Edmonds-Karp improves Ford-Fulkerson by choosing the augmenting path via BFS. Its time complexity is:
options: $O(VE)$
questions.explanation: Edmonds-Karp (BFS augmenting paths) runs in $O(VE^2)$: each augmenting path raises the shortest-path length monotonically, bounding the number of augmentations by $O(VE)$, each costing $O(E)$.

questions.prompt: In the network $s\to a$(3), $s\to b$(2), $a\to t$(2), $b\to t$(2), $a\to b$(1), what is the capacity of a minimum $s$-$t$ cut? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: By Max-Flow Min-Cut, min cut capacity equals max flow. From the previous computation max flow is $4$; the cut $\{s,a,b\}$ / $\{t\}$ has capacity $2+2=4$. So the minimum cut capacity is $4$.

questions.prompt: When no augmenting path exists from $s$ to $t$ in the residual graph, what can be concluded?
options: The algorithm must restart with a different source.
The current flow is maximum.
The network has a negative cycle.
Capacities must be fractional.
questions.explanation: If no $s$-$t$ augmenting path remains, the set of vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual graph defines a cut whose capacity equals the current flow, proving optimality by Max-Flow Min-Cut.

questions.prompt: Which problems can be modelled as and solved by maximum flow?
options: Maximum bipartite matching.
Maximum number of edge-disjoint $s$-$t$ paths.
Finding a maximum clique in an arbitrary graph.
Bipartite minimum vertex cover (via König's theorem).
questions.explanation: Bipartite matching, edge-disjoint paths, and (via König) bipartite min vertex cover are all flow-modellable. Maximum clique in a general graph is NP-hard (D false) and not solved by flow.

questions.prompt: In the undirected graph with edges $s{-}a, s{-}b, a{-}t, b{-}t, a{-}b$ (all capacity 1), what is the maximum number of edge-disjoint $s$-$t$ paths? Enter a single integer.
questions.explanation: The two obvious paths $s{-}a{-}t$ and $s{-}b{-}t$ are edge-disjoint (giving 2). Any third path would need to reuse an edge, so 2 is the maximum — equal to the max-flow value with unit capacities.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the capacity $c(e)$ of an edge and its flow $f(e)$?
options: They are always equal.
Capacity is the fixed upper bound; flow is the current amount pushed, satisfying $0 \le f(e) \le c(e)$.
Flow is the fixed upper bound and capacity varies.
Both are outputs of the algorithm.
questions.explanation: Capacity is part of the input (an upper bound), while flow is what the algorithm assigns, constrained by the capacity and by flow conservation. Only the flow is computed.

questions.prompt: Which statements about max flow are TRUE?
options: The total outflow from $s$ equals the total inflow into $t$ (the flow value).
At every internal vertex, total inflow equals total outflow.
The max flow value is at most the capacity of any $s$-$t$ cut.
Flow can exceed the capacity of an edge as long as conservation holds.
questions.explanation: Conservation (A, B) and the weak-duality fact that every flow is bounded by every cut (C) are true. Exceeding an edge's capacity (D) is a violation — capacities are hard constraints.

questions.prompt: How do you model a capacity limit on a **vertex** (not an edge) in a flow network?
options: You cannot; flow networks only have edge capacities.
Split the vertex $v$ into $v_{in}$ and $v_{out}$ with an edge $v_{in}\to v_{out}$ carrying the vertex capacity, routing all in-edges to $v_{in}$ and out-edges from $v_{out}$.
Set all edge capacities equal.
Add a self-loop.
questions.explanation: The standard node-splitting trick: replace $v$ by $v_{in}, v_{out}$ joined by an edge of the desired vertex capacity. This reduces vertex-disjoint path / node-capacitated problems to ordinary flow.

questions.prompt: For integer capacities bounded by $C$, how many augmenting paths can Ford-Fulkerson take in the worst case if each path can push only 1 unit?
options: At most $\log C$
At most $C \cdot E$
Exactly $V$
Exactly 1
questions.explanation: With integral capacities, each augmentation pushes at least 1 unit and the flow value is at most $C\cdot E$ (or use the min-cut bound), so the number of augmentations is bounded by the flow value — this is why choosing paths badly can be slow and why Edmonds-Karp (BFS) is preferred.

questions.prompt: When reducing a problem to max flow, which modelling choices are correct?
options: For bipartite matching, add a super-source to the left side (capacity 1 each) and a super-sink from the right side (capacity 1 each), with left-to-right edges of capacity 1.
For edge-disjoint paths, set every edge capacity to 1 and take the max flow.
For vertex-disjoint paths, split each vertex and set the split edge to capacity 1.
For maximum clique, connect a source to every vertex.
questions.explanation: Bipartite-matching, edge-disjoint, and vertex-disjoint constructions are all standard correct reductions (A, B, C). Maximum clique is NP-hard and has no flow reduction (D false).
